paragraphs: There was once a young man, strong and energetic, who could find no way to support his family. In the end he became a highway robber, attacking people on the roads and taking their money to feed his father, mother, wife and children. This went on for years, until one day the great sage Narada came walking by, and the robber pounced on him.

Narada asked him why he was doing this. Robbing and killing people was a terrible sin, he said, so for whose sake was he committing it? For his family, the robber replied. Did he think they would share the burden of his sin too? Of course they would, said the robber. Very well, said the sage: tie me up here so I can't escape, go home, and ask them whether they will share your sin the way they share your money.

The robber went first to his father and asked if he knew how his son supported him. The father didn't. When the son told him the truth, the old man was horrified and drove him out as an outcaste. His mother, hearing the same, was appalled, and refused to share any of the sin; she had never robbed anyone. His wife said the same: it was his duty as a husband to support her, and she would take no part in his wrongdoing.

The robber's eyes were opened. Even those closest to him, for whom he had done all this, would not share his fate. He hurried back, untied Narada, fell at his feet, told him everything and begged for help. The sage told him to give up his old life. His family loved him only for what he brought them; take that away and they would leave. No one shares our evil, though everyone will share our good. So, said Narada, worship the One who stands by us in both, whose love never pulls us down and asks nothing in return.

Narada taught him how to worship, and the man left everything and went into the forest. He prayed and meditated so deeply that he lost all awareness of himself; ants built their hills around his body and he never noticed. Many years later a voice called him to rise as a sage. Startled, he protested that he was a robber. The voice told him the robber was gone; he was now a purified sage. Because his meditation had been so deep that he had not even noticed the ant-hills, he would be called Valmiki, "born of the ant-hill." And so the robber became a sage.
learn: No past is too dark to change; one honest moment of self-reflection can turn a whole life around. It's also worth asking: whose approval are my choices really for, and would they stand by me in the consequences?
